paras: The attempted lynching of Jim Stevens took place in Charlottesville, Virginia, in the early morning of July 4, 1903, when about forty persons came close to lynching Stevens, a young Black man accused of robbing a trunk in a private residence. The threat arose from a rumor that he had attempted an assault, a charge the women of the house rejected. Stevens was later convicted of the robbery and sentenced to two years in the penitentiary.

According to a Charlottesville dispatch to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, Stevens entered the home of Joseph A. Peck on Second Street East at midnight and robbed the trunk of a woman from Richmond who was visiting the Peck family. The correspondent wrote that he lit the gas and went about the theft "very deliberately" until the women in the room woke and raised the alarm. Stevens escaped through a window and was afterwards arrested and identified.

A rumor then spread that he had attempted assault, and "for a time lynching looked certain" as about forty persons gathered. The women, however, "exonerated the man from that charge," and Stevens escaped the crowd. The coverage does not describe how the crowd was dispersed or whether officers intervened.

On July 29, 1903, Stevens, named in the later report as James Stevens, was found guilty of entering the Peck residence and robbing the trunk of a Richmond woman identified as Miss James. His term was fixed at two years in the penitentiary. No report of arrests or charges against members of the crowd was found.

The episode was reported by the Times-Dispatch's Charlottesville correspondent under the headline "A NEGRO'S NARROW ESCAPE" and the deck "Robbed a House and Came Near Being Lynched for Another Crime." The paper's Virginia news index repeated that framing, setting the house robbery apart from the rumored crime for which he was nearly lynched. The account made no comment on the crowd itself and called Stevens "a young negro" throughout.

On July 6 the Alexandria Gazette carried a shortened version in its "Virginia News" column that dropped the women's exoneration, leaving only the rumor and the near-lynching. When the Times-Dispatch reported the conviction on July 30, it noted in an index item and a short dispatch that Stevens had "narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of a mob" over the assault rumor. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The same-day dispatch placed the crowd "at an early hour this morning" on July 4, while the follow-up dated the mob to July 3. The break-in occurred at midnight on the night of July 3-4, and the July 4 dispatch, written within hours, is the closer source.

bases: A crowd of about forty persons threatened to lynch Stevens after a rumor of attempted assault spread, and he 'narrowly escaped lynching' (A2, A5).
About forty persons threatened Stevens over a rumored attempted assault, a group acting without authority on a crime accusation, but he was not killed (A2, A5).

accounts.label: Charlottesville correspondent
accounts.gist: Stevens allegedly entered the Peck house, lit the gas and rifled a visitor's trunk; the ladies woke, he fled through a window and was later arrested; a rumor of attempted assault brought about forty persons near to lynching him, but the ladies exonerated him of that charge.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'A NEGRO'S NARROW ESCAPE' and stressed that he 'Came Near Being Lynched for Another Crime', separating the robbery from the false assault rumor without comment on the crowd.
The Alexandria Gazette ran a condensed copy in its 'Virginia News' column, dropping the ladies' exoneration.

versions.value: Early morning of July 4, after a midnight break-in

conflicts.note: The break-in was at midnight on the night of July 3-4, which may explain the follow-up's date; the July 4 dispatch, written the same day, places the crowd 'at an early hour this morning'.

record_check.dossier: Accused of house-entering and trunk robbery; attempted assault was only a rumor, and the ladies exonerated him of it

record_check.record: He escaped and was later arrested.
record_check.dossier: He escaped the house through a window before his arrest; the papers do not describe how he escaped the crowd. He was convicted of the robbery on July 29 and given two years in the penitentiary
July 4 per the same-day dispatch; the follow-up says July 3
